description: Hi. We are an international team that came to Valencia just for this Hackathon! We cover areas from business to computer science, and interest in building a technical solution that will leave an impact for everyone.
summary:
"Through the Cloud" is an open web app and data pipeline that turns data from NISAR, the new NASA-ISRO radar satellite, into stories anyone can follow about how land changes: floods, crops and fire. NISAR sees the ground through cloud and at night every 12 days, anywhere on Earth. 

Our case study is Valencia, Spain, where we are based and where floods in 2024 and 2026 hit towns we know. 

The app answers three questions. What does the radar see: a vision model maps water on every pass. Did the official flood maps point to where the water really went: we checked them against two real floods, town by town and street by street. Where is water likely next: a model trained on two years of satellite water maps, terrain and rain gives a likelihood for every 20 m pixel. A small game lets visitors guess where a marsh will flood before the storm and then shows the radar pass that followed. This matters because in the 2024 flood, 58% of the damaged buildings and 59% of the flooded street length we checked lay outside every official flood zone. Every result is scored against a simple baseline and published with its limits, including where our own models lose. All inputs but the official zones are global and open, so the method can move to any region.
details:
Through the Cloud is a full pipeline from raw NISAR radar data to a web app with no backend. NASA's Harmony service cuts each site out of the NISAR GCOV files (L-band, HH and HV, 20 m), and every layer is placed on one shared grid. A small U-Net ensemble finds open water in each scene, trained on same-day OPERA DSWx-S1 water maps at three wetlands and tested on two sites it never saw. A per-pixel classifier labels land by how it behaves through the season (rice, water, forest, burned, urban). A gradient-boosted model (LightGBM) then gives each pixel a likelihood of being wet on a coming pass, from height above the nearest drainage, elevation, slope, land cover, water history, the latest water map and rain. It was trained on 413 Sentinel-1 water maps per site, with the storm month held out. Results are baked into small Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs and JSON that the browser reads directly.

The app has five parts: the flood at the Pego-Oliva marsh before and after the storm of October 2026 (DANA "Adam"), the rice season at the Albufera, where fields are flooded on purpose, the wildfire scar in Serra d'Espadà, a street map that overlays the official flood zones on what really flooded, with surveyed water depths and our model, and a game where the player predicts the flood and learns from the next radar pass.

The benefit is an honest public check of flood maps. In the 10 towns hit on 29 October 2024, 46 % of the flooded land, 58 % of the 2,238 affected buildings and 59 % of the flooded street length lay outside every official flood zone. At Pego-Oliva in 2026 the official map was right for 95 % of the flooded land. Our prediction model ranks newly flooded pixels better than terrain alone or past wetness (average precision 0.47 against 0.41 and 0.33 at the Albufera). We also report where our methods lose: terrain flow alone did not beat the official zones, the vision model fails at one test site, and the prediction reacts weakly to the rain amount. It is a map of where water tends to go, not a warning system.

Valencia is the case study, not the limit. Every input except the official flood zones is global and open: NISAR, OPERA water maps, the Copernicus terrain model, ESA land cover and ECMWF rain. A new site is a bounding box in one configuration file, and we already ran the pipeline on seven sites in Spain and France. The models must be retrained for each region, which the pipeline does from the same open data, and the comparison with official maps works wherever a country publishes its flood zones. We chose depth over breadth: one region, tested honestly, with the method ready to move.

We built it with Python (rasterio, xarray, PyTorch, LightGBM, scikit-learn), NASA Harmony and earthaccess, Next.js, TypeScript and MapLibre GL. The project is creative in joining a brand-new radar mission with a game and street-level stories, so that someone who has never heard of SAR can use it. We considered scientific rigour first: test rules were written down before any score was computed, the storm month was held out of the prediction model's training, and every map says what it cannot show. At 20 m, radar cannot see water between buildings, and the app says so.
